Performance Skills in the Exam

In Section A of your written drama exam, you will be asked how an actor would use voice and physicality to communicate meaning. You need to know the specific terminology for each skill and be able to apply it to characters and moments in Blood Brothers. You also need to understand semiotics — how signs and symbols on stage create meaning for the audience.

Voice Skills — The CTPAPVE Mnemonic

Use the mnemonic “Clever Tony Plays Pitch And Putt Virtually Everyday” to remember the eight voice skills. The initial letters spell out:

Key Fact — Voice Skills

Clarity — how clearly the actor speaks so the audience can understand every word. Tone — the emotional quality of the voice (e.g. warm, cold, sarcastic, desperate). Pace — how fast or slow the actor speaks. Pitch — how high or low the voice is. Accent — the regional or social way of speaking (e.g. a Liverpool accent for Mickey, Received Pronunciation for Edward). Pause — a deliberate silence for dramatic effect. Volume — how loud or quiet the actor speaks. Emphasis — stress placed on a specific word to change meaning.

How voice changes between characters and between Acts:

  • Edward (child): Received Pronunciation (RP) accent to show his wealthy background. Enthusiastic tone, fast pace, and clear voice to show confidence and eagerness when meeting Mickey.
  • Mickey (child): Liverpool accent reflecting his working-class Liverpool roots. Louder volume and faster pace to show energy and streetwise confidence.
  • Mickey (adult, post-prison): Quiet volume, slow pace, flat tone to show his depression. Emphasis on “him” when saying “I could have been him!” to communicate envy and resentment.
  • Mrs Lyons (Act Two): Higher pitch, faster pace, more strained tone to show her increasing paranoia and instability.
  • The Narrator: Controlled pace, low pitch, sinister tone. Deliberate pauses before key words to build tension. Clear and measured delivery to maintain authority.

Physicality Skills

Use the mnemonic “Head Shoulders Knees and Toes” (thinking about the whole body) to remember that physicality covers everything from head to toe. The key terms are:

Key Fact — Physicality Skills

Eye contact — who the character looks at and when. Facial expression — what the face communicates (joy, fear, anger). Posture — how the character holds their body (upright, slumped, tense). Muscle tension — how tight or relaxed the body is. Gesture — specific hand or arm movements to communicate meaning. Body language — overall physical communication (open, closed, defensive). Gait — how the character walks (confident stride, shuffling, hurried). Levels — whether the character is standing, sitting, crouching, or elevated. Proximity — the distance between characters on stage.

How physicality changes between characters and between Acts:

  • Edward (child): Open body language showing sincerity. Upright posture showing confidence. Happy facial expressions, enthusiastic gestures. Moves towards Mickey (close proximity) to show eagerness.
  • Mickey (child): Energetic gait, animated gestures, relaxed muscle tension. Wide stance and confident posture despite his poverty — he is streetwise and bold.
  • Mickey (adult, post-prison): Slumped posture, shuffling gait, minimal gestures, high muscle tension. Avoids eye contact. Keeps a bigger distance from other characters. Low levels — he may sit or hunch while others stand.
  • Mrs Lyons (Act One): Upright posture, controlled gestures, tight body language. In Act Two, she becomes physically erratic — wild gestures, pacing, invading Mrs Johnstone’s space.
  • The Narrator: Controlled, deliberate movements. Often positioned at a higher level or on the periphery of the action, watching. Still posture that contrasts with the emotional chaos of other characters.

Semiotics — Creating Meaning on Stage

Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols. In drama, everything on stage is a sign that communicates meaning to the audience — from the colour of a costume to the direction of a spotlight. Russell uses semiotics throughout Blood Brothers:

  • Colour symbolism — Mickey’s red jumper links to the Labour Party and working-class identity; Edward’s blue links to the Conservative Party and wealth
  • Set symbolism — doors, levels, and the use of the stage floor all communicate status and access
  • Sound symbolism — the singular magpie cackle represents sorrow; the heartbeat represents stress
  • Proxemics — characters move closer to the audience when they want empathy, and further away when they know what they are doing is wrong
  • Lighting symbolism — colour washes, gobos, and spotlights all carry meaning beyond simply illuminating the stage
  • Costume symbolism — fabric quality, colour, and condition all signal class, mood, and character arc

The COSTUMES Acronym

For any design question in the exam, use the COSTUMES acronym to structure your answer. This works for costume, set, lighting, and sound questions:

Key Fact — The COSTUMES Framework

Context — what is the character’s situation? Opinion — in my opinion, I would… Style — what is the style of the production? Time Period — when is the play set? Uber (location) — where is the scene taking place? Materials — what materials, fabrics, or equipment would be used? Examples from the text — reference a specific moment. Semiotics — what meaning does your choice communicate to the audience?

Stage Directions

Stage directions are written instructions for actors and designers. In Blood Brothers, they serve three purposes:

  • Practical information — whether a character is singing or speaking
  • Motivation — for example, “a satisfied smile by Linda” implies she was pleased to impress Mickey when shooting the air pistol
  • Emotion — for example, “Mrs Johnstone runs frantically” tells us about her state of mind

In the exam, you can use stage directions as evidence. If asked how an actor would perform a scene, the stage directions give you Russell’s intended emotions and motivations, which you can then translate into specific voice and physicality choices.

Proxemics — the use of distance on stage — is one of the most powerful tools an actor has. In Blood Brothers:

  • Close proximity — Mickey and Edward stand close when they first become friends, showing their instant bond. Mrs Lyons invades Mrs Johnstone’s space to show manipulation and control.
  • Distance — Mickey moves away from Linda and Edward in Act Two, showing emotional withdrawal. Mrs Johnstone stands far from Mrs Lyons when she knows the secret is dangerous.
  • Proximity to the audience — the Narrator moves close to the audience when foreshadowing events, breaking the fourth wall. Mrs Johnstone comes to the apron for “Tell Me It’s Not True,” drawing the audience into her grief.

In the exam, you may be given a specific line and asked how an actor would deliver it. Follow this structure:

Example: Edward says “Do you want to be my friend?”

  • Accent: RP accent to show Edward comes from a wealthy background.
  • Tone: Enthusiastic tone to show he is lonely and genuinely wants to make friends.
  • Clarity: Clear voice to show he is a confident young man.
  • Body language: Open body language to show sincerity.
  • Facial expression: Happy facial expressions to show excitement about making a new friend.

Notice how each point names the skill, describes how it would be used, and explains why — what it tells the audience about the character.
